newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay shares close lower as reliefs fail to cheer.
newsitem.headline: Bombay shares close lower as reliefs fail to cheer.

text.p: Bombay shares ended lower on Monday when incentives announced by Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram failed to cheer sentiment, traders said.
"The incentives aren't of much immediate use to investors so the market is unlikely to run away," one trader said.
On Friday, Chidambaram removed a 30 percent ceiling on investment in debt by foreign institutional investors.
He exempt investments in mutual funds from capital gains tax, upped the ceiling marginally on tax-spared dividend income and doubled the limit for bank advances against shares to one million rupees.
But market reaction was muted with traders saying the reliefs fell below expectations.
They said investors were expecting more reliefs when the minister wraps up a delayed budget debate later this week.
"There are no one-time or magic solutions," Chidambaram told parliament in the first stage of his budget reply on Friday.
"But I am persuaded that there is urgent need to perk up market sentiment since a good part of market behaviour is based on psychology and sentiment," he said.
Chidambaram will address parliament again this week before the budget for 1996/97 (April-March) is put to vote.
Brokers are expecting him to dilute a 12.9 percent minimum tax on profits of firms and offer other tax incentives.
In its latest strategy report Lehman Brothers said it is overweight on the Indian market from a 12-month perspective.

"The situation currently is that liquidity is ample and relative yields are moving in favour of equities from a domestic investor perspective and with a forecast decline in interest rates and a pick up in economy later this year," it said.
"The outlook for equities is positive," Lehman said forecasting a 12-month target of 4750 points for the Bombay index.
